lines.text: Do you know how Starlink works? A hundred miles out at sea, no towers, no signal, and this ship is still streaming video.
A cell tower only reaches a few dozen kilometers. Out here, the nearest one is far over the horizon.
So the ship carries this. A flat white Starlink dish. It doesn't tilt or turn to chase satellites. It doesn't need to.
Inside are hundreds of tiny antennas. Fire them a split second apart, and the beam bends toward any satellite. No moving parts.
Up there are over six thousand Starlink satellites, each about the size of a car, just five hundred and fifty kilometers up.
That low, they race around the Earth in about ninety-five minutes. So the dish keeps handing you from one satellite to the next.
Old satellite internet sat thirty-six thousand kilometers away. Over half a second there and back. Starlink is usually under fifty milliseconds.
Near land, the satellite beams your data straight down to a ground station, plugged into the internet.
But mid-ocean, there's no station below. So the satellites pass your data to each other, with lasers.
And in space, light travels about fifty percent faster than through the glass fibers under the sea.
Hop, hop, hop, until a satellite is above land. Then down it goes, and you're online.

It works on planes too. At cruising height, cell towers can't reach your phone, because their signals point at the ground. So airlines like United and Qatar Airways put a Starlink antenna on the roof, and the whole cabin gets Wi-Fi.
And some phones now skip the dish entirely. With T-Mobile's T-Satellite, a normal phone can text and use some apps, straight from a Starlink satellite.
And once you're online, even in the middle of the ocean, Orbi Transfer works too. Your file is locked before it ever leaves the ship.
Orbi Transfer dot com. Now you know!
